title: Linking adrenal and immune function biomarkers with management factors to assess welfare in captive tigers (Panthera tigris) in Thailand
content:
Abstract
Captive tiger welfare is shaped by the combined effects of housing, husbandry and management, yet the use of physiological measures in welfare assessments of this species remains limited. This study developed a management-based composite index to summarize cumulative housing and husbandry conditions in captive tigers and evaluated its biological relevance using repeated measures of adrenal and immune biomarkers. Faecal samples were collected at ~3-month intervals over 1 year from 224 captive tigers housed at three wildlife-tourism facilities in Thailand for analysis of faecal glucocorticoid metabolites (fGCM) and faecal immunoglobulin A (fIgA). The index integrated eight management variables representing structural, spatial, social, dietary, tourist-contact and staffing conditions. In the primary adjusted mixed-effects models, higher index values were associated with lower fGCM concentrations (β = −0.22 ± 0.08; P = 0.008), but not with fIgA concentrations (β = −0.31 ± 0.47; P = 0.506). At the individual-factor level, yard access, yard size and staff-to-tiger ratio were associated with lower fGCM, whereas no individual management variable was significantly associated with fIgA. By comparison, clinical disease was associated with fIgA but not with fGCM; tigers with gastrointestinal conditions had higher fIgA concentrations than those classified as clinically normal. The two biomarkers showed a weak positive observation-level correlation and remained positively associated after covariate adjustment. Sampling period was associated with both biomarkers, and temporal patterns differed among facilities. These findings indicate that the two biomarkers reflected management and clinical variation differently. The management-based composite index, interpreted alongside endocrine, immune and clinical measures, may provide a structured framework for biologically informed welfare monitoring in wildlife-tourism settings.
